la:verb:augeo.gloss: to increase, augment, enlarge, spread, expand
senses: to increase, augment, enlarge, spread, expand
la:verb:augeo.html:
augĕo, auxi, auctum, 2, v. a. and n. (
perf subj. auxitis = auxeritis, : auceta: saepe aucta, Paul. ex Müll.; v. Müll. ad h. l.) [Gr. αὔξω αὐξάνω; Lith. augu, and augmu = growth; Sanscr. vaksh; Goth. vahsjan, and auka = growth; Germ. wachsen; Engl. wax; also allied to vegeo vegetus, vigeo vigor, vigil

v. Curt. pp. 67, 186 sq., and Bopp, Gloss. p. 304 b].

Act., to increase, to nourish (orig., to produce, bring forth that not already in existence; in which signification only the derivative auctor is now found).
To increase, enlarge, augment, strengthen, advance that which is already in existence (class. in prose and poetry; syn.: adaugeo, amplio, amplifico): Quicquid est hoc, omnia animat, format, alit, auget, Pac. ap. : cibus auget corpus alitque,: redductum (animale genus) daedala tellus alit atque auget generatim pabula praebens,; ; ; 6, 946: virīs,: in augendā re,; ; so, in augendā obruitur re,: rem strenuus auge,increase your gains,: opes,: possessiones,: divitias,: dotem et munera,: rem publicam agris,; so : aerarium,: vallum et turres,: classem,: tributa,: pretium,: numerum,, and : morbum,: suspitionem,; : industriam,: molestiam,: dolorem alicui, vitium ventris, : peccatum,: furorem,: benevolentiam,: animum alicujus, to increase one's courage, ; so, animos,: vocem,to strengthen, raise,; ' hostias, to increase, multiply, : ego te augebo et multiplicabo,—Poet.: nuper et istae Auxerunt volucrum victae certamine turbam,i. e. have been changed into birds,.—
Trop., to magnify, to exalt, to extol, embellish, to praise (syn.: laudo, laude afficere, verbis extollere, orno): homo tenuis non verbis auget suum munus, sed etiam extenuat,: aliquid augere atque ornare,; so, rem laudando,: munus principis,—
Aliquem (aliquid) aliquā re, to furnish abundantly with something, to heap upon, give to, to enrich, endow, bless, load with: lunae pars ignibus aucta, the part that is entirely filled with fire, Lucr 5, 722: 3. 630: Tantā laetitiā auctus sum, ut nil constet, poët, ap. oaque vos omnia bene juvetis, bonis auctibus auxitis, old form of prayer in : alter te scientia augere potest, altera exemplis,the one can enrich you with learning, the other furnish you with examples,: aliquid divitiis,: commodis,: senectus augeri solet consilio, auctoritate, sententiā,: gratulatione,: honore,: honoribus,; so : honoribus praemiisque,; : augeri damno, to be enriched with a loss (said comically), : liberalitate,: largitione,: nomine imperatorio,: cognomento Augustae, et saep.—Also without abl.: Di me equidem omnes adjuvant, augent, amant,, and : aliquem augere atque ornare,to advance,: aut augendi alterius aut minuendi sui causā aliquid dicere, solum te commendat augetque temporis spatium, honors, ; so ; .—
In the lang. of religion, t. t. (like mactare, adolere, etc.), to honor, reverence, worship by offerings: Aliquid cedo, Qui vicini hanc nostram augeam aram [Apoliinis],: si quā ipse meis venatibus auxi, etc.,.—
Neutr., to grow, increase, become greater (rare; syn.: augesco, cresco, incresco; on this use of vbs. com. act., v. Ellis ad ): eo res eorum auxit, Cato ap. : usque adeo parcunt fetus augentque labore,: ignoscendo populi Romani magnitudinem auxisse, (Fragm. Orat. Philipp. contra Lepid. § 6): O decus eximium magnis virtutibus augens,: balnea Romae ad infinitum auxere numerum,; : veram potentiam augere, (Halm, augeri).—Hence, auctus, a, um, P. a., enlarged, increased, great, abundant; in posit. only as subst.: auctum vocabatur spatium, quod super definitum modum victoriae adjungitur, Müll. —Comp.: tanto mi aegritudo auctior est in animo,: auctior est animi vis,: auctior et amplior majestas,; ; : auctius atque Di melius fecere,.—* Sup.: auctissima basis, Treb. Gall. 18.—Adv. probably not in use, for in Oud., altius is the correct reading.
la:verb:augeo.inflection: auxi, auctum, 2, v. a. and n.

la:noun:augur.gloss: augur (priest, diviner, or soothsayer, one who foretold the future in part by interpreting the song and flight of birds)
senses: augur (priest, diviner, or soothsayer, one who foretold the future in part by interpreting the song and flight of birds)
la:noun:augur.html:
augur, ŭris (earlier also auger, P.), comm. (cf. Prob. p. 1455 P., and Phoc. p. 1695 P.) [avis and Sanscr. gar, to call, to show, make known. Van.],
an auqur, diviner, soothsayer; at Rome, a member of a particular college of priests, much reverenced in earlier ages, who made known the future by observing the lightning, the flight or notes of birds, the feeding of the sacred fowls, certain appearances of quadrupeds, and any unusual occurrences (v dirae).
Lit.: Interpretes Jovis optumi maxumi, publici augures,; Fest. s. v. quinque, p. 26 Müll.; ; and others cited in Müll. Etrusk. 2, p. 116 sq., and Smith, Dict. Antiq. (diff. from auspex, orig. as a general idea from a particular one, since the auspex observed only the flight of birds; cf. . Yet as this latter kind of augury was the most common, the two words are frequently interchanged or employed in connection; cf. Enn. ap. : dant operam simul auspicio augurioque).—
Transf., any soothsayer, diviner, seer, in gen.: augur Apollo, as god of prophecy (v. Apollo), ; so, augur Phoebus,: Argivus,i.e. Amphiaraus,; ; : veri providus augur Thestorides,i. e. Calchas,; ; ; 3, 349; 3, 512 al.: nocturnae imaginis augur,interpreter of night-visions,: pessimus in dubiis augur timor,fear, the basest prophet,.—Fem.: aquae nisi fallit augur Annosa cornix,: simque augur cassa futuri!; ; ; : augures caeli,.

senses: to perform the services of an augur, interpret omens, augur

la:noun:augurium.html:
augŭrĭum, ii, n. (plur. augura, heterocl., like aplustra from aplustre, Att. ap. , or Trag. Rel. p. 217 Rib.) [augur],
the observation and interpretation of omens, augury (v. augur and the pass. there cited).
Lit.: pro certo arbitrabor sortes oracla adytus augura? Att., Trag. Rel. p. 217 Rib.: agere, Müll.; ; : capere,: quaerere,: observare,; : non est augurium in Jacob,: dare,: nuntiare,: decantare,: accipere, to understand or receive as an omen, ; ; : augurium factum,: augurio experiri aliquid,: augurium salutis, an augury instituted in time of peace, for the inquiry whether one could supplicate the Deity for the prosperity of the state (de salute), ; ; ; cf. Dio Cass. 37, 24, and Fabric. ad h. l.—
Transf.
Any kind of divination, prophecy, soothsaying, interpretation: auguria rerum futurarum,: conjugis augurio (by the interpretation of

quamquam Titania mota est, : Divinatio arroris et auguria mendacia vanitas est, Vulg Eccli. 34, 5.—And transf. to the internal sense. presentiment, foreboding of future occurrences inhaeret in mentibus quasi saeclorum quoddam augurium futurorum, ; : Fallitur augurio spes bona saepe suo,: Auguror, nec me fallit augurium, historias tuas immortales futuras,—

Object, a sign, omen, token, prognostic: thymum augurium mellis est,: augurium valetudinis ex eā traditur, si etc.,.—
The art of the augur, augury: cui laetus Apollo Augurium citharamque dabat, (v. Apollo and augur): Rex idero et regi Turno gratissimus augur,; .

la:adj:augustus.html:
augustus, a, um, adj.
from augeo, as angustus from ango; v. augeo
, originally belonging to the language of religion,
majestic, august, venerable, worthy of honor (class. in prose and poetry; in Cic. mostly in connection with sanctus; never in Plaut., Ter., Lucr, or Hor.; syn.: magnus, venerabilis, venerandus): sancta vocant augusta patres: augusta vocantur Templa, sacerdotum rite dicata manu,: Πάντα γὰρ τὰ ἐντιμόταγα και τα ἱερωτατα Αὔγουστα προσαγορευεται, Dio Cass. 53, 16: augurium, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 494 Vahl.): Cives ominibus faustis augustam adhibeant Faventiam, Att. ap. , and p. 357, 15 (Trag. Rel. p. 202 Rib.): Eleusis sancta illa et augusta,: sanctus augustusque fons,: Liber, qui augusta haec loca Cithaeronis colis, auct. inc., Trag. Rel. p. 268 Rib.: locus augustus,: templum,; : augustissimo et celeberrimo in templo,: fanum,: solum,: moenia, (augurio consecrata, Serv.); so, gravitas (caelestium),; : mens, et saep.— Transf. to other things (so most freq. after the Aug. per.): tectum augustum, ingens,.—Of bees: sedes, (augustum: abusive, nobile, quasi majestatis plenum, Serv.): ut primordia urbium augustiora faciat, Liv. praef § 5: habitus formaque viri, id 1, 7, 9; so, species,: conspectus,: ornatus habitusque,: augustissima vestis,: augustior currus,: augustissimum tribunal, al.—Adv.: augustē, reverently, sacredly: auguste sancteque consecrare, auguste sancteque venerari, .—Comp non quo de religione dici posset augustius, .—Sup. prob. not in use

senses: of August, the sixth month of the Roman calendar

la:other:Augusta.gloss: an honorific title given to the wives of Roman Emperors
senses: an honorific title given to the wives of Roman Emperors
The name of several ancient towns, such as Augusta Praetōria (modern day Aosta), Augusta Taurīnōrum (modern day Turin) or Augusta Vindelicōrum (modern day Augsburg)
la:other:Augusta.html:
Augusta, ae, f. (dat. Augustal) [augustus].
Under the emperors, a litle of the mother, wife, daughter, and sister of the emperor; like our Imperial Majesty, Imperial Highness, Tac A. 1, 8; 15, 23; 4, 16; 12, 26; , 10; 15; 23; ; , ; cf. Schwarz.—
The name of several towns, among which the most distinguished were,
Augusta Taurinorum, now Turin, ; ; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 191.—
Augusta Praetoria, in Upper Italy, now (by a corruption of the word Augusta) Aosta, ; ; cf. Mann. Ital. I. p. 186 sq.—
In Treveris Augusta, now Treves, (colonia Treverorum, ).—
Augusta Vindelicorum, now Augsburg, Itin. Anton.; cf. , n. 4 Rupert.—
Augusta Emerida on the Anas, in Lusitania, now Merida, ; cf. Mann. Hispan. p. 331.

la:verb:augesco.gloss: to (begin to) grow, develop or increase
senses: to (begin to) grow, develop or increase
la:verb:augesco.html:
augesco, ĕre,
v. inch. [augeo], to begin to grow, to become greater, to grow, increase (syn.: cresco, incresco); lit. and trop.: qui rem Romanam Latiumque augescere vultis, Enn. ap, Acron. ad (Ann. v. 455 Vahl.): mare et terrae,; ; ; 5, 251; 5, 334; 6, 616: semina,: quibus animantes alantur augescantque,; ; : augescunt corpora dulcibus atque pinguibus et potu,; : augescente flumine,: mihi cotidie augescit magis De filio aegritudo, * : Jugurthae Bestiaeque et ceteris animi augescunt,: occurrendum augescentibus vitiis,; : augescente licentiā,: augescente superstitione,

la:noun:augmentum.html:
augmentum (in MSS. also augŭ-mentum), i, n.
augeo
,
an increase, growth, augmentation (very rare; mostly post-Aug.).
Lit.: augmentum corporis,: crescit in augmentum Dei,: augmentum aut deminutio,: fundi,: lunae,—Plur.: dabit capiti tuo augmenta gratiarum,; .—
In the lang. of religion (cf. augeo, I. C.), a kind of sacrificial cake, Müll.; so (where others read augmina).

la:adj:auguralis.html:
augùrālis (augŭrĭālis, App. Not. Aspir. § 8), e, adj.
augur
.
Of or belonging to augurs, relating to soothsaying or prophecy, augurial: libri,; ; cf. Müll. Etrusk. 1, p. 122: jus,: cena,which the augur gave on his entrance into office,, : insignia, Liv 10, 7: sacerdotium,; : verbum,.—Hence,
Subst.: augŭrāle, is, n.
A part of the headquarters of a Roman camp, where the general took auguries: structam ante augurale aram,: egressus augurali,.—Hence (pars pro toto), the principal tent: tabernaculum ducis, augurale,.—
The augur's wand or staff = lituus, .

la:verb:auguror.html:
augŭror, ātus. 1, v. dep. (class. for the ante-class. and poet.
act. augnro, āre, v.infra) [augur].
To perform the services or fill the office of an augur, to take auguries, observs and interpret omens, to augur, prophesy, predict (hence with the acc. of that which is prophesied): Calchas ex passerum numero belli Trojani annos auguratus est,; so ; : avis quasdam rerum augurandarum causa esse natas putamus,; ; : in quo (scypho) augurari solet,: augurandi scientia,; .—Transf from the sphere of religion,
Ingen, to predict, forebode, foretell; or of the internal sense (cf. augurium, II. A.), to surmise, conjecture, suppose: Theramenes Critiae, cui venenum praebiberat, mortem est auguratus,: ex nomine istins, quid in provinciā facturus esset, perridicule homines augurabantur,: in Persis augurantur et divinant Magi,: Recte auguraris de me nihil a me abesse longius crudelitate, Caes. ap. , A: futurae pugnae fortunam ipso cantu augurantur,: quantum ego opinione auguror,: quantum auguror coniectura,. 95; so, mente aliquid, Curt 10, 5, 13: Hac ego contentus auguror esse deos,: erant, qui Vespasianum et arma Orientis augurarentur,: Macedones iter jaciendo operi monstrāsse eam (beiuam) augurabantur,.!*? The act. subordinate form auguro, āre (by Plin. ap. , erroneously distinguished from this in signif.).
(Acc. to I.) Sacerdotes salutem populi auguranto, .—Trop.: oculis investigans astute augura, look carefully around you like an augur, Plant. Cist. 4, 2, 26.—Pass.: res, locus auguratur, is consecrated by auguries: certaeque res augurantur, Lucius Caesar ap. P.: in Rostris, in illo augurato templo ac loco,; so : augurato (abl. absol.), after taking auguries (cf. auspicato under auspicor fin.): sicut Romulus augurato in urbe condenda regnum adeptus est,; dub. Roth.—
(Acc. to II.) Hoc conjecturā auguro, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 327 Vahl.); so Pac. ap. Non. l. l.; Att. ib.; Fragm. ib. (p. 431 Moser): praesentit animus et augurat quodam modo, quae futura sit suavitas, id. Ep. ad Caiv. ib. (IV. 2, p. 467 Orell.): si quid veri mens augurat,: quis non prima repellat Monstra deum longosque sibi mon auguret annos?.
